headline: China's Most Precipitous Mountain, Captured in 17.79 Megabytes
lede: A creator known as mr3dgs has published a navigable, photorealistic three-dimensional scan of Huashan — China's Western Sacred Mountain — to SuperSplat, a web platform for *3D Gaussian Splats*. The scene compresses a mountain of legendary inaccessibility into under 18 megabytes of data, deliverable in any modern browser. The bookmark's author, @abstrakt314, posted it as a simple act of admiration; there is more under the surface.
body:
A user known only as mr3dgs has posted a *3D Gaussian Splat* of **Huashan** — the Western Sacred Mountain of China — to SuperSplat, a web platform run by PlayCanvas, a subsidiary of Snap Inc. (SNAP). Captured by drone and weighing a spare 17.79 megabytes, the scene renders Huashan's vertiginous granite peaks and Taoist temple clusters in navigable, photorealistic three dimensions. The scene has drawn nearly ten thousand views in its first month.

The underlying technology, **3D Gaussian Splatting** (3DGS), was introduced by Bernhard Kerbl and colleagues at INRIA in a paper presented at ACM SIGGRAPH in August 2023. Rather than encoding a scene in a neural network — as *Neural Radiance Fields* (NeRF), the prior dominant technique, do — 3DGS represents the world as millions of semi-transparent ellipsoids, each carrying position, colour, and opacity. The renderer skips neural inference entirely, splattering those ellipsoids onto the screen via GPU *rasterization* and achieving over 100 frames per second at 1080p on consumer graphics hardware, against NeRF's typical 10–30. The explicit representation also captures view-dependent lighting effects — reflections, atmospheric haze, the sheen of lichen on cliff faces — that traditional *photogrammetry* pipelines, which produce textured polygon meshes, tend to flatten away.

SuperSplat is run by PlayCanvas, a London-based studio acquired by Snap Inc. (SNAP) in 2018. Its CEO, Will Eastcott, completed a transition to fully open-source infrastructure in April 2025, releasing the viewer under the MIT licence and noting that the 3DGS community had made impressive strides through open collaboration. The platform offers in-browser editing, format conversion, and social publishing, with recent additions including walk mode, level-of-detail streaming, and SuperSplat Studio — an authoring layer for annotated spatial experiences. It is an unusual genealogy: the platform best positioned to become the archive of the physical world is a subsidiary of a mobile social-media company under considerable financial pressure.

Huashan — the “Flower Mountain” — sits 120 kilometres east of Xi'an in Shaanxi Province and holds the Western position among China's *Five Sacred Mountains* (五岳, Wuyue), an ancient cosmological arrangement in which the cardinal peaks organized imperial ritual relations with heaven. Its South Peak reaches 2,154.9 metres, and its cliffs are so sheer that a traditional proverb holds there is only one path up the mountain. That path includes the Plank Walk — wooden boards bolted to near-vertical granite with iron chains as the sole handhold — widely considered one of the world's most dangerous hikes. The character 华 in Huashan also appears in 中华 (Zhonghua) and 华夏 (Huaxia), the oldest names for Chinese civilisation; this mountain is, in a real etymological sense, a root of China's self-conception.

Mr3dgs appears to be based in Xi'an: their other published scenes include Datang Everbright City, a Tang-dynasty-themed cultural district in the city, suggesting a deliberate focus on the heritage of the former imperial capital. The scene's file size is itself a technical achievement: raw 3DGS output runs to gigabytes, but SuperSplat now supports *SOGS* — a compressed format developed by PlayCanvas that achieves roughly twenty-fold size reduction — bringing a mountain range within reach of ordinary web delivery. Peer-reviewed studies published in 2025 confirm that drone-based 3DGS preserves surface patina, weathering, and material qualities that mesh-based photogrammetry loses. As heritage institutions from the Smithsonian onward explore the format, the work of independent creators like mr3dgs — scanning places that institutional programmes have not yet reached — carries an archival weight that casual enthusiasm tends to understate.

concepts.definition: A technique for representing and rendering real-world scenes, introduced at ACM SIGGRAPH 2023. It encodes a scene as millions of semi-transparent 3D ellipsoids (Gaussians), each carrying colour and opacity, which are projected onto the screen in real time via GPU rasterization. Unlike neural-network-based methods, it requires no inference step and achieves over 100 frames per second on consumer hardware.

A technique for synthesising novel views of a scene by training a neural network to predict colour and density at any point in 3D space. Introduced in 2020, NeRF produces photorealistic results but renders slowly — typically 10–30 fps — because every pixel requires querying the network many times. 3DGS largely supplanted it for interactive applications.

The process of reconstructing a three-dimensional scene from overlapping photographs, producing a textured polygon mesh. It is the dominant method for architectural surveying and heritage digitisation, offering high geometric accuracy, but it tends to miss view-dependent lighting effects like reflections and atmospheric translucency.

A set of five mountains in China — one at each cardinal direction plus the centre — that held ritual and cosmological significance for Chinese emperors from antiquity onward. State sacrifices were offered at each as a way of aligning the dynasty with the natural order. Huashan is the Western mountain; Taishan in the east is the most ceremonially prominent.

The process by which a GPU converts three-dimensional geometry — points, triangles, or in 3DGS, ellipsoids — into a two-dimensional image by projecting each primitive onto a pixel grid. It runs on dedicated silicon and is extremely fast, which is why 3DGS can render at real-time frame rates unlike methods that require per-pixel network inference.

A compressed file format for 3D Gaussian Splat scenes, developed by PlayCanvas and open-sourced in 2025. It achieves roughly twenty-fold reduction in file size compared with uncompressed 3DGS output, making large photorealistic scans practical for ordinary web delivery. PlayCanvas adopted it as the platform's default format after demonstrating the compression gains on real-world scenes.
